p.x:
I live in Bangkok, and the traffic here can be terrible. When I started my job, I drove my car to work every day. The road was always busy, and the journey took more than an hour. It was very slow, and petrol was expensive.
Now I take the subway. It is fast and cheap, and I can read a book on the way. The station is only five minutes from my home. Sometimes, when it rains, I take a taxi to the station.
My friend Lek has an electric scooter. She says it is quiet and easy to park. My brother rides his bike, but he says there aren't enough cycle lanes in our city. One day, I want to try a plane to Chiang Mai instead of the bus, because it's much quicker!

Imagine sitting in a car that drives itself. You could read, sleep or watch a film while the car takes you to work. Driverless cars are no longer science fiction. In several cities in the USA and China, ride-sharing companies already use them to carry passengers.
These cars use sensors and cameras to see the road, other cars and people. A computer decides the speed and the best route, and it can change lanes safely. Most of them are electric, so they produce no emissions from the engine, and they stop at a charging station when their battery is low. The range of newer models is over 400 kilometres.
Supporters say driverless cars will reduce accidents, because computers don't get tired or drunk. However, some people are worried. What happens if a sensor fails? And will taxi drivers lose their jobs?
Meanwhile, other ideas are being tested too: drones that deliver parcels, high-speed trains, and even flying cars. The way we travel may look very different in twenty years.

Transport produces around a quarter of the world's carbon emissions, so a transition to cleaner travel is essential if countries are to become carbon-neutral. Electric vehicles are leading the way, but they are only part of the solution.
Many governments offer subsidies or tax incentives to encourage people to adopt electric cars. In Norway, these policies have been so successful that most new cars sold are now electric. Critics, however, point out that subsidies mainly benefit wealthier buyers, and that electricity generated from coal is hardly clean.
For heavy transport such as lorries and ships, batteries may be too heavy, so engineers are exploring hydrogen fuel. Meanwhile, ambitious projects like the hyperloop, which would send passenger pods through low-pressure tubes, promise speeds of over 1,000 km/h, although many experts doubt whether they are economically feasible.
Fully autonomous vehicles raise further questions. If a self-driving car causes an accident, who bears liability: the owner, the manufacturer or the software company? Laws in most countries have not yet answered this.
Perhaps the most effective changes are the least glamorous. Investing in trams, rail and safe streets for walking can improve mobility for everyone, including those who cannot afford a car.
